blocks.t: Elegy works on two levels: mechanics and narrative. The mechanics are the gamey part, involving dice and resources like Rush or Health. The narrative is the story part: what your character does, what happens around them, and how the plot unfolds. The two work together. Your narrative flows freely until it hits a moment that needs a mechanical resolution. Once resolved, the dice’s outcome shapes what happens next. Asking the Oracle When you have questions about what happens next, what you discover, or how characters respond, you may always go with what feels right and pick the most obvious or interesting result. blocks.t: The Action Roll

When you need to resolve an uncertain or risky situation related to your character’s efforts, you make an action roll. Action rolls all follow the same structure, described below. Most rolls you make in Elegy are action rolls. A few very specific rolls may use different structures, but they are always explained where they appear. To make an action roll, roll your action die (1d6) and two challenge dice (2d10). Action Die Challenge Dice
Results
The result of your roll depends on how many challenge die your action score beats.

items.t: If your action score beats both challenge dice, it’s a Stylish Success. You get what you want, the way you want.
If it beats only one, it’s a Flat Success. You get what you want, but with side effects, reduced effectiveness, or a moderate cost.
If it beats neither, it’s a Failure. Your assumptions were wrong, a brief triumph costs too much, or you simply fail.

Rush Paying the Price

Rush represents your inertia and confidence, and how sure you are of your actions. The value ranges from -6 to +10. You use Rush to improve the result of an action roll: after making one, if your Rush is higher than your action score, you may cool your Rush to replace your action score with your current Rush value. When you do, reset your Rush to the value of your base Rush (+2 by default). This value, as well as your max Rush, may change if your character uses certain abilities, or is transformed through her experiences.

blocks.t: Basic Actions

Below you’ll find prompts for the most common actions your character may attempt. They follow the same structure, but each has results and details tailored to a specific situation. Basic Actions exist to guide your narrative with minimal friction: each one offers ready-made interpretations of your roll, so you can see at a glance what happens (or doesn’t) in that specific context. If you’d rather skip these prompts and use a single, one-size-fits-all mechanic, you can use the Generic Action Roll instead. It works just like the Basic Actions, only in a broader, less prescriptive way, making it ideal for quicker resolutions.

Blood represents your animating force and satiation gained from consuming blood. The lower it is,
the hungrier you become, and the closer you are to being taken over by instincts or even stop moving. When you wake up or use a supernatural ability, you lose Blood according to what you’re doing.
FLOW YOUR BLOOD
When you channel the blood within your corpse to activate a supernatural power or endure the day, lose Blood as prompted and roll with the prompted Attribute.
Stylish Success: The effect is activated. Gain +1 Rush if using an Aspect.
Flat Success: The effect is activated, but lose 1 Blood.
Failure: The effect is activated, but at a high cost. Lose 1 Blood and pick one:

items.t: It strains your body: lose 1 Health.
It strains your mind: lose 1 Clarity.
It wastes time, has an inconvenient side-effect, or puts you in a bad position: lose 1 Rush.

blocks.t: APPEAR ALIVE

When you restore the appearance of a living body, Flow Your Blood with Soul. For the rest of the scene, add +1 to every roll you make by acting as a regular mortal. You don’t need to roll again if you already activated this power this scene.
SLUMBER

When the sun rises, you slip into the death-sleep. Lose 1 Blood (can’t be mitigated) and gain +1 Rush. If you violated a law or custom of vampire society tonight, Try Your Standing. To instead stay awake through the day, lose 2 Blood and Flow Your Blood with Soul. On any Success, you remain awake for one day scene. When the scene ends, you must sleep or do this again. When you slumber, also write a lingering question as a Loose End (see Experience, later in this chapter).

Conscience

Your Conscience represents your contact with your human nature, principles and mindset. It’s not tracked through a meter, but actions that harm it may make you suffer lasting conditions, or even become a mindless beast.
TRYING YOUR CONSCIENCE

At the end of a scene where you take a life or bloody a Connection, roll with Soul to try how your Conscience reacts. If you killed in self-defense or to protect someone else when no other option remained, treat a Failure as a Flat Success.
Stylish Success: You push through: gain +1 Rush.
Flat Success: As above, but a weird feeling hits you: lose 1 Clarity.
Failure: You reach your limit; suffer the first unmarked condition in the cascade below.

items.t: Detached: You are more willing to cross your moral boundaries; until the end of next night, treat your Soul as 1 point lower. When next night ends, you recover: erase the condition.

Penitent: You are struck by intense guilt and a desire for redemption. Commit to a Mission of Rank 4 to repent in favor of a greater good. Until you fulfill it, reduce your max Rush by 1. When you do, you recover: erase the condition.
Blighted: Your human essence falters, and vampirism tightens its grip. Mark the condition Blighted, then pick a Burden Aspect representing the weakness you develop.

blocks.t: If all conditions above are marked, you are completely dominated by your instincts: see The End, at the end of this section.
Standing

Your Standing represents your reputation and standing among your peers, especially your authorities. Like Conscience, it’s not tracked through a meter, but can still cause lasting conditions or end your story.
TRYING YOUR STANDING
At the end of a night where you violated the laws or customs of vampire society, roll with Charm to maintain your standing among your authorities. Actions that trigger this roll may include:

items.t: Breaking the laws or customs of the ruling authority
Showing disrespect or defiance toward an elder or superior
Exposing vampire secrets to outsiders
Leaving a witness or unfinished business that could expose the community
Failing or refusing a duty assigned by vampire authority
Acting against the interests of a faction that holds power over you

blocks.t: Stylish Success: They turn their eye or let it slide. Next night, it’s like nothing happened. Gain +1 Rush.
Flat Success: They let it pass, but uncomfortably. Next night, you might feel an air of awkwardness between you and authorities, but nothing serious. Gain no Rush.
Failure: They condemn and punish you. You awaken to the written warning from an authority you disrespected; suffer the first unmarked condition in the following cascade.

items.t: Cautioned: You are told to step in line. Reduce your max Rush by 1 until next time you slumber. When you do, you recover: erase the condition.

Discredited: Your standing has eroded and you are expected to prove your worth. Reduce max Rush by 1, then create a progress track of Rank 3. When you deliberately act in service of that authority and get any Success, mark progress. When the progress track is complete, your respect is restored. Erase the condition.

Branded: Your repeated transgressions are brutally punished with a permanent symbol of betrayal. You awake not to a written warning, but to a group of vampires in service of your authority, who then personally brands you with fire. Acquire the burden Branded.

blocks.t: If all conditions above are marked, you are captured by dusk, forced into an open space, and left to die when the sun comes up: see The End, at the end of this section.
The End

When your story ends, in your last moments, the memory of a meaningful event from your life crosses your mind for the first and only time since your death: Ask the Oracle for a Theme and envision what you remember.

Connections
Creating a Connection
When you start a new relationship with a useful or important character, or when you narratively
establish one you already had, you create a Connection. On your Connection sheet, write their name
and give them an appropriate Rank (see below). Connections are Aspects, and can be upgraded with XP.
Making Progress in a Connection
When you reinforce your relationship with a Connection by…

items.t: …committing to a Mission in their service…
…completing a Mission that benefits them…
…relying on their help in desperate circumstances…
…sharing a profound and meaningful moment together…
…standing by them through hardship…
…overcoming a test of your relationship…

blocks.t: …mark progress in the Connection according to its Rank. When you fill the whole track, your Connection is Sealed, and now you have a relationship of honest mutual trust: gain experience per the Rank of the Connection. When you would make progress in a Connection that’s already Sealed, gain +2 Rush instead.
COMMON NPC RANKS
* Werewolves are one Rank higher when transformed.
Testing a Connection
When a Connection is tested through conflict, betrayal, or circumstance, roll with Soul if they’re mortal or Charm if they’re not. If Sealed, add +1.
If you have no interest in maintaining the relationship, treat it as a Failure.
Stylish Success: This test brings you closer. Make progress in the Connection.
Flat Success: As above, but also envision a demand or complication as a fallout and pay the price.
Failure: They demand proof of your loyalty. Pick one:

items.t: You drink their vampiric blood, and the connection gets bloodied by them (see below)

They require something in the form of a Mission of the same Rank as theirs +1 (if not already 5). Until you see it done, take no benefit for the Connection. If you refuse or fail, the Connection is permanently undone.

blocks.t: Bloodying a Connection
When vampiric blood is shared between you and a Connection, it becomes Bloodied.
BLOODIED BY YOU

When you let someone drink from your veins, you bind them emotionally to you: create a Connection with them if you don’t already have one. Then, make progress in the Connection, and mark it as Bloodied by you. At the end of the scene, Try Your Conscience for this act.
When you interact with a connection that’s Bloodied by you, roll one extra action die and pick the best.
BLOODIED BY THEM

When you drink from another vampire’s veins, you become emotionally bound to them: create a Connection if you don’t already have one, and mark it as Bloodied by them. If you drank against your will, the Connection has no dots or Feats: it’s not a real relationship and grants no bonuses. Acting against a Connection Bloodied by them goes against your deepest impulses: when you roll against them, subtract their Rank.
Adventuring with Connections

A Connection may sometimes accompany you into dangerous Missions as a partner, lackey, or ally. When they do, create a Pulse meter for them on your Character Sheet. Their standard maximum Pulse equals their Rank +2. When a Connection takes damage, they lose Pulse just as you would lose Health. You may also envision your Connection taking a hit as the Price of an action roll when it fits the moment.
REACHING THEIR LIMITS
When a Connection has 0 Pulse and loses more, roll your dice and add their Rank (instead of any Attribute) as they avoid destruction.
Stylish Success: Recover 1 Pulse.
Flat Success: As above, but also lose 1 Rush.
Failure: They are out of action until you heal them. On a match, they are dead or destroyed.
HEALING YOUR CONNECTION
You can restore a Connection’s Pulse three ways:

items.t: Slumbering. When you slumber, they recover Pulse equal to their Rank.
Giving them your blood. Restore their Pulse by 1, 2, or 3 and lose the same amount of Blood. If the Connection wasn’t already Bloodied by you, it becomes so (see above).
Letting them heal. When a Connection stops for several minutes to heal, roll your dice and add their Rank instead of an Attribute.

blocks.t: Stylish Success: They recover their Rank in Pulse.
Flat Success: They recover half their Rank, rounded up, in Pulse.
Failure: They recover half their Rank, rounded down, but the situation also worsens. Pay the price.

Picture what this city is like, then fill out the following details on your World Sheet:

items.t: Name: what is your city called officially?

blocks.t: • Founded in: write a date, year, century, or even historical period.

items.t: Economy: what are the main industries and economic activities?
Climate: subtropical? Temperate? Polar? Something else?
Language(s): what are the official languages?
Highlights: what lures mortals into this city?
Ugly side: what makes them leave?

blocks.t: For the highlight and ugly side, you may roll on the following tables or use them for inspiration. Every

c: A dominant industry fuels the city’s economy. Workers move here from across the region for employment, and local culture is built around this industry.
Ruins, museums, and monuments from a past era are everywhere. Tourism feeds on them, academia studies them, and the city’s identity is shaped by that period.
What era defines it, and what ruins or archeological pieces are the most famous?
Nights are as active as days. Most services run around the clock, and the city never fully quiets down. People eat, shop, commute, and socialize at any hour.
What type of commerce can rarely be found open?
Bars, clubs, live music venues, and late-night gathering spots define the city’s reputation. Entire neighborhoods exist to serve the nightlife.
What is the most famous nightlife spot in this city?
The city has a deep history of art production, exhibition, and trade. Art fairs are held here regularly, galleries are part of the urban landscape, and artists move here to be taken seriously.
What kind of art is it known for?
One or more university campuses are major references in the region. Many come here specifically to study, and academic events are frequent and diverse.
What academic field is the city most famous for?
Citizens’ rights are enforced through public programs. Inequality exists, but visibly less than elsewhere.
What reflection of that can you see every night that is mindblowing to outsiders?
The city is well preserved, well maintained, and frequently adopts newer technology in public spaces. Streets are clean, transit works, public buildings are functional.
What public structure (roads, metro lines, hospitals, public housing, etc.) is the most famous for how well it works?
Life is much less dangerous here than elsewhere. Outsiders are shocked at how easily you can walk the streets, especially at night.
What public safety measures allow this?
The natural environments within or surrounding this city are unlike anything else. People from across the world come here to see them, and they shape the city’s identity and tourism.
The industry that once sustained this city collapsed. A large portion of it is now crumbling, and crime grows in the emptied areas.
What new industry is being attempted here?
Tourism has consumed the economy. Residents can’t afford to eat where they live or rent where they grew up. The city’s identity is performative for strangers, and authenticity lies elsewhere.
What “traditional” experience do tourists seek the most here?

Privacy has been gutted, allegedly for security. The government can access any medium of communication and scan it at will. No message transmitted here is actually secret, and self-censorship is the norm.
What device, platform, or medium do people use to communicate secretly?
The city is too big for its own good. Everything is far away, commutes are enormous, and transportation is expensive.
What service do app drivers usually offer on the side to please their clients?
You can’t drink the tap water. Gutters overflow in strong rains, and any body of water near a populated neighborhood smells like a sewer, because it is one.
What body of water do you know that actually smells fine?
Every public service has been sold off. Government programs go to the cheapest bidder, better alternatives exist only for those who can pay, and none of the public options work properly.
Which privatized service causes the most daily frustration?
Breathing here is bad for your health. Streets smell of exhaust, smog is frequent, and nights are brighter because street lights reflect off the haze.
What do residents usually do to protect themselves?

Much of the city is divided into territories controlled by heavily armed gangs. They run the illegal services, and disagreements are resolved violently, in the open. Residents know which streets belong to whom.
What do they trade in? Game? Vice? Illegal media?

The city’s politics are decided by organized crime families, out in the open. They present themselves as protectors and do provide stability, but those who oppose them are dealt with brutally and publicly.
What horrendous method of execution is applied to enemies and traitors?

The city is plagued by one or more animal species that are never properly dealt with and always return. Infestations are common, the animals appear on the streets, and every extermination campaign fails within months.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD FIRST MISSION?

items.t: Make it personal. Why does this matter to your character?
Make it unavoidable. This problem won’t solve itself; it demands a response.
Add urgency. The situation will get worse or slip away if ignored.
Raise the stakes. If it feels too small, layer in complexity, consequences, or emotional tension.
Keep the scope tight. Focus on something manageable that could unfold in one or two sessions.

blocks.t: MULTIPLAYER

If you’re playing with allies (other player characters), this becomes a shared mission. Collaborate to create the incident and ensure it connects with your group’s goals and dynamics. If you’re the game master (GM), introduce a compelling incident based on character and world details, or guide the group in co-creating one so that everyone is invested.
Step 2: Set the Scene
Once your mission is chosen, decide how to begin.
OPTION 1: PROLOGUE

Start slow. Show your character during a typical night: hunting, meeting acquaintances, enjoying the nightlife, or handling routine tasks. Use this to build character and relationships before the real action begins. After a few scenes, introduce an inciting incident or a request from a Connection that kicks off the mission.
OPTION 2: IN MEDIAS RES
Start in the middle of the action. The problem has already begun, and your character is already reacting. You’re diving straight into the thick of it. Things are already in motion.
Step 3: Commit to a Mission
Write down the mission and assign it a Rank:

items.t: Rank 1: a simple or minor task.
Rank 2: a challenging but unremarkable task.

blocks.t: First missions should be Rank 1 or 2; higher Ranks are for later in the story.
Step 4: Next Steps

After committing to your mission, consider the context. Is the path clear? Did new questions arise? Is something now standing in your way? From here, play to discover. Ask questions. React to developments. Roll dice when needed. When in doubt, ask the Oracle. Don’t worry about getting everything right. Mistakes and uncertainty are part of learning. Keep your reference sheets handy, improvise when needed, and keep the game moving.

Gifts are groups of vampiric powers, including mind control, shapeshifting, or commanding animals. You can naturally develop up to three, but may acquire more by learning from other vampires. Each ability is a different power.

NPCs (non-player characters) are everyone in the world who isn’t you or your fellow players (your allies). You roleplay interactions and attempt to influence, aid, gain help, or act against them. In Elegy gameplay, your character’s abilities and actions take center stage, and NPCs are portrayed mainly through fiction rather than mechanics. They have only one mechanical stat, their Rank, which represents their durability in combat, skill and influence. When NPCs appear in your story or assist you in facing challenges, focus on how they shape the story and your decisions. Treat them as real characters, not just tools: give them quirks, desires, and a voice. Use the Oracle to guide their choices, reactions, and performance. They might help or hinder you. They might be charming, unreliable, loyal, or dangerous. Let them evolve as the story unfolds, but always keep the spotlight on your character and their closest allies.
Creating NPCs

Build NPCs that fit your city and world. You can start with sample NPCs from this chapter or invent your own. Because NPCs don’t require stats beyond Rank, they’re quick and easy to bring to life. Imagine who they are, what they want, and how they might act, and play from there. If you’re not sure, consult the Oracle for clues about their nature or intentions. Then, decide what feels true to the fiction. NPCs may become long-term presences in your story. When they stick around, take notes about what you’ve learned about them, especially if you create a Connection. This chapter provides sample NPCs organized by category, offering many starting points.
